intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that cerebellar ataxia, impaired intellectual development, and dysequilibrium syndrome-4 (CAMRQ4) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the ATP8A2 gene (605870) on chromosome 13q12.

paragraphs.text: Cerebellar ataxia, impaired intellectual development, and dysequilibrium syndrome-4 (CAMRQ4) is a rare early-onset neurodevelopmental disorder. Its features are nonprogressive cerebellar ataxia, intellectual disability of varying severity, hypotonia, dysarthria, and cerebellar atrophy, and some patients walk on all fours (quadrupedal locomotion). Severity ranges from congenital ataxia with near-normal cognition and independent walking to severe disease with involuntary movements, optic atrophy, feeding difficulty, and no head control (Onat et al., 2013; Mohamadian et al., 2020; Damásio et al., 2021; Narishige et al., 2022).

paragraphs.text: Mohamadian et al. (2020) reported 3 sibs with CAMRQ4 from a consanguineous Iranian family of Arab descent; the parents were first cousins. The proband was a 9-year-old girl who had severe hypotonia as a newborn. All her psychomotor milestones were delayed, and she used a wheelchair because she could not walk, sit, or hold up her head. She had had feeding difficulties since infancy. Her affected brother and sister, aged 17 and 15 years, had similar features. All 3 patients had IQ levels of 20 to 40, delayed speech and language, dysarthria, and absent deep tendon reflexes, but no significant hearing impairment. Brain MRI showed cerebellar atrophy in all 3, and metabolic studies were normal.

paragraphs.text: Narishige et al. (2022) reported 2 Japanese sibs with CAMRQ4 who developed athetotic movements at 1 and 2 months of age. Both also had ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, feeding difficulty, hypotonia, and severely delayed development, and one had retinal degeneration and optic atrophy. Over time they developed areflexia and flattened auditory brainstem responses. At last follow-up, neither patient could sit or control the head, although some nonverbal communication was preserved. The disease did not progress in early development, which the authors noted could make it hard to tell apart from dyskinetic cerebral palsy.

paragraphs.text: Onat et al. (2013) studied a consanguineous Turkish family with CAMRQ4. Homozygosity mapping, followed by targeted next-generation sequencing of 1 affected member, identified a homozygous missense mutation in the ATP8A2 gene, ile376-to-met (I376M). The authors supported the variant with segregation analysis, population screening, and prediction programs. The mutation lies in a highly conserved C-terminal transmembrane region of the E1-E2 ATPase domain. Onat et al. (2013) also pointed to an unrelated person with intellectual disability and severe hypotonia who carried a de novo balanced t(10; 13) translocation that disrupts ATP8A2.

paragraphs.text: Mohamadian et al. (2020) studied 3 sibs with CAMRQ4 from a consanguineous Iranian family. Whole-exome sequencing of the proband identified a homozygous c.1339G-A transition (NM_016529.6) in exon 14 of the ATP8A2 gene, causing a gly447-to-arg (G447R) substitution. Sanger sequencing confirmed the mutation. All 3 affected sibs were homozygous, while both parents and 2 unaffected sibs were heterozygous and 1 unaffected sib did not carry it. The mutation was absent from public variant databases and from 100 healthy controls of the same ethnicity. It changes a conserved residue in the ATP-binding domain. In silico structural modeling predicted that it lowers protein stability and alters the ligand-binding pocket.

paragraphs.text: Damásio et al. (2021) studied 2 sibs with a relatively mild form of congenital ataxia. Exome sequencing identified a homozygous c.1580-18C-G change in intron 17 of the ATP8A2 gene, which was predicted to create a new splice acceptor site. In a minigene assay in HEK293T cells, the mutant construct produced an abnormal transcript that kept 17 bp of intron 17. This in-frame insertion of 4 amino acids leads to a premature stop codon.

paragraphs.text: In affected members of a consanguineous Turkish family with CAMRQ4 and quadrupedal locomotion, Onat et al. (2013) found a homozygous ile376-to-met (I376M) mutation in the ATP8A2 gene. The mutation was identified by homozygosity mapping and targeted next-generation sequencing, and the authors supported it with segregation analysis, population screening, and prediction programs. It lies in a highly conserved C-terminal transmembrane region of the E1-E2 ATPase domain. Mohamadian et al. (2020) gave the nucleotide change as c.1128C-G.

paragraphs.text: In 3 sibs with CAMRQ4 from a consanguineous Iranian family, Mohamadian et al. (2020) found a homozygous c.1339G-A transition in exon 14 of the ATP8A2 gene, causing a gly447-to-arg (G447R) substitution. The mutation was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. It segregated with the disorder: both parents and 2 unaffected sibs were heterozygous. It was absent from public databases and from 100 ethnically matched controls. The substitution affects a conserved residue in the ATP-binding domain, and in silico modeling predicted that it lowers protein stability and alters the ligand-binding pocket.

paragraphs.text: In 2 sibs with congenital ataxia and near-normal cognition, Damásio et al. (2021) found a homozygous c.1580-18C-G change in intron 17 of the ATP8A2 gene by exome sequencing. In a minigene assay in HEK293T cells, the change created an alternative splice acceptor site. The resulting transcript kept 17 bp of intron 17, inserting 4 amino acids and causing a premature stop codon.
